New Holland honeyeaters (Phylidonyris novaehollandiae) exhibit a clear sexual size dimorphism in their ultimate body mass, an important metric for understanding life history trade-offs. Adult males typically attain a maximum body mass of 20.2 grams [Wwi = 20.2 grams], whereas adult females reach a slightly lower asymptotic mass of 18.5 grams [Wwi = 18.5 grams]. This difference is linked to distinct reproductive roles, with males requiring robust condition for territorial defence and courtship display. The species begins life as a rapidly developing altricial chick, with newly hatched nestlings weighing only 2.56 grams [Ww0 = 2.56 grams], a remarkably small initial wet weight relative to the adult size. This initial mass is supported entirely by the yolk reserves and early parental provisioning, setting the stage for a steep growth trajectory during the nestling period.

The incubation period for these honeyeaters is temperature-dependent, with eggs maintained at a constant 32 °C [T = 32 °C] in controlled studies hatching after 14 days [ab = 14 days]. This incubation length is typical for a passerine of this body size and reflects the trade-off between embryo development rate and the energetic cost of brooding. Upon hatching, the naked, altricial chicks are entirely dependent on parents for temperature regulation and food delivery. The precise temperature control during artificial incubation ensures that the 14-day developmental timeline from egg to hatchling is achieved, yielding a neonate that is physiologically prepared for the intensive feeding phase that follows.

Under normal field conditions, when the ambient temperature during active periods reaches 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a predictable sequence of post-hatching events unfolds for the nestlings. Fledging, the milestone at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight, occurs at 16.5 days after hatching [tx = 16.5 days after hatching] under these thermal conditions at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid development from hatchling to flying juvenile is characteristic of many honeyeaters and is energetically demanding, requiring high rates of parental food delivery. The time since birth at fledging is comparatively short, reflecting the species' strategy of producing multiple broods within a single favorable season and minimizing the window of nest vulnerability.

Sexual maturation in Phylidonyris novaehollandiae is a slower process. At the same body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the age at which young birds attain puberty is 49.5 days after hatching [tp = 49.5 days after hatching]. This time since birth at puberty marks the point when gonadal development is complete and the bird is physiologically capable of reproduction, although actual breeding is often deferred until the following season. The interval between fledging and puberty is a period of intense foraging and skill acquisition, during which juveniles accumulate the body condition necessary for the subsequent high-energy demands of courtship, nest building, and egg production.

Reproductive output in this species is modest but consistent. Females typically lay 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch] and produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. Consequently, the annual reproductive output is approximately 2.5 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2.5 eggs per year]. The time since birth at first brood, measured under the typical thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning first-time breeders do not initiate a nest until their second calendar year. This one-year delay is consistent with many small passerines that require an entire year to establish territory and gain foraging experience before investing in reproduction. The oldest documented individuals in the wild have been recorded reaching a maximum lifespan of approximately 11.9 years [am = approximately 11.9 years], a longevity that permits multiple breeding seasons at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Energetic demands during reproduction are high, and respirometry trials have measured a basal metabolic rate of 57.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 57.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour] for a 20.1 g adult at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reflecting the substantial metabolic machinery required to sustain this life history.
